sources: Penn State Extension, Yellow Garden Spider (Argiope aurantia): females 19-28 mm, males 5-8 mm; webs 50-100 cm in diameter are not uncommon; a white zigzag stripe down the centre, the stabilimentum, whose exact function is unclear; people are not likely to be bitten unless they handle a female with an egg sac in the web, and a bite would cause no more discomfort than a wasp or bee sting for most people; not medically important; papery egg sacs laid in late summer, 500-1,000 spiderlings emerge in early spring; https://extension.psu.edu/yellow-garden-spider

Missouri Department of Conservation, Field Guide: Black-and-Yellow Garden Spider: harmless; circular web about two feet across with a vertical zigzag silk band; females 3/4 to 1 inch, males about 1/4 inch and rarely noticed; makes its web vibrate when disturbed; eats mostly grasshoppers and katydids; papery tan egg cases a little smaller than ping-pong balls that can contain over 1,000 eggs each; the female slows and dies in the first frosts; https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/black-yellow-garden-spider

National Wildlife Federation, Wildlife Guide: Yellow Garden Spider: venom harmless to humans; stabilimentum purpose unknown, it may warn birds away from the web; may eat and respin its web each night; males usually die after mating; https://www.nwf.org/Educational-Resources/Wildlife-Guide/Invertebrates/Yellow-Garden-Spider

beats.say: A huge black and yellow spider just strung a web across your garden path, up to three feet wide.
Walk too close, and it shakes its whole web at you.
The yellow garden spider. With a thick white zigzag in the middle.
Does it have venom? Yes. But its venom is for bugs, like grasshoppers.
It only bites if you handle it. And for most people, that feels like a bee sting.
How to tell? A big black and yellow body, and that zigzag.
And nobody knows for sure what the zigzag is for.
